Q: What does 'channel width' refer to in wireless networking?
Option1: The physical width of an antenna
Option2: The frequency span a channel occupies (for example, 20/40/80/160 megahertz)
Option3: The number of access points in a building
Option4: The height of a wireless tower

Q: Which statement best describes non-overlapping channels?
Option1: Channels that have the highest power output
Option2: Channels that do not share frequency spectra and therefore minimize adjacent-channel interference
Option3: Channels reserved only for emergency services
Option4: Channels used only in the 6 GHz band

Q: In the 2.4 GHz band, which set lists the commonly used non-overlapping channels in most regions?
Option1: Channels 2, 7, and 12
Option2: Channels 1, 6, and 11
Option3: Channels 3, 8, and 13
Option4: Channels 4, 5, and 9

Q: What is the main purpose of the standard known as 802.11h?
Option1: To define wireless names and passwords
Option2: To provide radar avoidance and power control (dynamic frequency selection and transmit power control) in 5 GHz bands
Option3: To require the use of virtual private networks on guest networks
Option4: To enable mesh networking between routers

Q: Which scenario best fits choosing a narrower channel width (for example, 20 megahertz) over a wider one?
Option1: You need the highest possible single-client throughput on an empty spectrum
Option2: You want to minimize interference and fit more clean channels in a congested environment
Option3: You are designing a short-range point-to-point bridge
Option4: You must support only legacy wired clients

Q: Why might a wider channel width (for example, 80 or 160 megahertz) be undesirable in a busy office?
Option1: It increases encryption overhead
Option2: It decreases the basic service set identifier range
Option3: It uses more spectrum and is more susceptible to interference from neighboring access points
Option4: It prevents roaming between access points

Q: Which frequency band is typically most congested due to many consumer devices like microwaves and Bluetooth?
Option1: 2.4 GHz
Option2: 5 GHz
Option3: 6 GHz
Option4: 10 GHz

Q: Which frequency band generally offers the greatest number of non-overlapping channels for high-density deployments (with compatible hardware)?
Option1: 2.4 GHz
Option2: 5 GHz
Option3: 6 GHz
Option4: 3 GHz

Q: Compared with 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz typically provides:
Option1: Longer range and better wall penetration
Option2: Fewer channels but better propagation
Option3: More channels and less interference, but shorter range and poorer wall penetration
Option4: Identical characteristics in all environments

Q: What is band steering?
Option1: Automatically forcing all devices to use 2.4 GHz
Option2: Encouraging dual-band clients to join higher-capacity bands (5 or 6 GHz) to reduce congestion on 2.4 GHz
Option3: Switching clients to cellular data when Wi-Fi is busy
Option4: Blocking legacy clients from joining the network

Q: What is a Service Set Identifier (SSID)?
Option1: The media access control address of a radio
Option2: The human-readable name that identifies a wireless network
Option3: The encryption algorithm used by the network
Option4: The channel number for 5 GHz networks

Q: What is a Basic Service Set Identifier (BSSID)?
Option1: A human-readable network name shared by multiple access points
Option2: A unique identifier (typically the radio’s media access control address) for a single access point radio
Option3: A list of channels available in a country
Option4: A password used for enterprise authentication

Q: What is an Extended Service Set Identifier (ESSID)?
Option1: A per-radio identifier used for roaming decisions
Option2: The identifier for a collection of access points broadcasting the same network name to form one logical wireless network
Option3: A temporary guest network identifier
Option4: An antenna model number

Q: Relationship: How do SSID, BSSID, and ESSID relate?
Option1: SSID and BSSID are identical values; ESSID is unrelated
Option2: SSID is the readable network name; each radio that serves it has its own BSSID; the same SSID across multiple radios forms an ESS (extended service set) identified by the ESSID
Option3: BSSID names the network; SSID identifies the radio; ESSID is optional and unused
Option4: ESSID is only used for guest portals; SSID/BSSID are for private networks

Q: Which network type uses peer-to-peer links without an access point?
Option1: Infrastructure
Option2: Ad hoc
Option3: Mesh network with controller
Option4: Point-to-multipoint cellular

Q: Which network type uses multiple access points to extend a single wireless network for client access?
Option1: Infrastructure
Option2: Ad hoc
Option3: Point-to-point
Option4: Personal area network

Q: Which description best fits a wireless mesh network?
Option1: Two radios connected by an ethernet cable
Option2: Multiple wireless nodes forwarding traffic for each other to extend coverage or backhaul
Option3: A single radio with a high-gain directional antenna
Option4: A network that requires no configuration

Q: Which scenario is ideal for a point-to-point wireless link?
Option1: Connecting two buildings across a parking lot using directional antennas
Option2: Providing general client access inside an office
Option3: Roaming support inside a warehouse
Option4: Providing cellular backup for a branch

Q: What is Wi-Fi Protected Access 2 (WPA2)?
Option1: A guest portal technology
Option2: A wireless encryption and authentication standard based on Advanced Encryption Standard with pre-shared key or enterprise modes
Option3: A 5 GHz channel plan
Option4: A type of antenna

Q: What improvement is central to Wi-Fi Protected Access 3 (WPA3) compared with Wi-Fi Protected Access 2?
Option1: It removes encryption to improve speed
Option2: It introduces Simultaneous Authentication of Equals for stronger password-based authentication and improved protections against offline guessing
Option3: It requires all access points to be mesh nodes
Option4: It uses only the 2.4 GHz band

Q: Which statement compares Wi-Fi Protected Access 2 and Wi-Fi Protected Access 3 correctly?
Option1: Both require open authentication only
Option2: Wi-Fi Protected Access 3 strengthens authentication and security features relative to Wi-Fi Protected Access 2
Option3: Wi-Fi Protected Access 2 is stronger than Wi-Fi Protected Access 3
Option4: They are unrelated to wireless security

Q: What is a captive portal?
Option1: Automatic channel selection on an access point
Option2: A web page that intercepts new client connections for acceptance of terms, login, or payment before granting network access
Option3: A method of dynamic frequency selection
Option4: A portal that converts wireless to wired traffic

Q: Which configuration is best for a visitor network that should not access internal resources?
Option1: Enable Wi-Fi Protected Access 3 only
Option2: Create a dedicated guest virtual local area network with a captive portal and isolation from production networks
Option3: Use the same network as employees with a different password
Option4: Use open authentication without any restrictions

Q: What does 'Pre-shared Key (PSK)' mean in wireless authentication?
Option1: Each user logs in with a unique certificate
Option2: All clients share a single passphrase to join the network
Option3: Authentication is performed by a third-party cellular provider
Option4: Users are authenticated by their device media access control addresses only

Q: In 'Enterprise' wireless authentication, clients are typically verified by which mechanism?
Option1: A single shared passphrase
Option2: IEEE 802.1X (port-based network access control) using a Remote Authentication Dial-in User Service server for per-user credentials
Option3: A captive portal without credentials
Option4: Open authentication with no encryption

Q: When should Enterprise authentication be preferred over Pre-shared Key?
Option1: In very small home networks only
Option2: When you need per-user credentials, centralized control, and auditing at scale
Option3: When devices cannot support encryption
Option4: When you want to allow anonymous access

Q: What is an omnidirectional antenna?
Option1: An antenna that radiates energy in one narrow direction only
Option2: An antenna that radiates roughly evenly in all horizontal directions
Option3: An antenna used only indoors
Option4: An antenna that requires cellular backhaul

Q: What is a directional antenna?
Option1: An antenna with an even radiation pattern in all directions
Option2: An antenna that focuses energy into a narrower beam for longer distance or point-to-point links
Option3: An antenna that changes bands automatically
Option4: An antenna used only for guest networks

Q: You must link two rooftops one kilometer apart. Which antenna choice is best?
Option1: Omnidirectional on both ends
Option2: Directional antennas aimed at each other
Option3: Internal laptop antennas only
Option4: No antennas are required

Q: Which statement describes an autonomous access point?
Option1: A radio that depends on a central controller for configuration and control
Option2: A standalone access point that is configured and managed individually
Option3: A device that only supports mesh backhaul
Option4: A device that cannot broadcast an SSID

Q: Which statement describes a lightweight access point?
Option1: A standalone access point with a built-in controller
Option2: A radio that offloads most control and management to a separate wireless controller
Option3: A device used only for point-to-point links
Option4: A device that supports wired routing only

Q: When might a lightweight access point architecture be favored over autonomous?
Option1: In a tiny office with one access point
Option2: When centralized policy, roaming optimization, and scalable management are required across many access points
Option3: When there is no controller available and each device must be configured separately
Option4: When no encryption is desired

Q: Clients crowd the 2.4 GHz band even though 5 GHz coverage exists. What feature should you tune first?
Option1: Captive portal settings
Option2: Band steering to encourage capable clients to 5 GHz
Option3: Directional antenna alignment
Option4: Disable encryption

Q: Your office experiences frequent disconnections when weather radar is active on nearby frequencies. Which standard or setting is most relevant?
Option1: Disable all 5 GHz radios
Option2: Apply 802.11h functions such as dynamic frequency selection and transmit power control
Option3: Switch to 2.4 GHz only
Option4: Use captive portals for all clients

Q: A warehouse needs maximum single-client throughput for scanning stations with little nearby Wi-Fi. Which choice is best?
Option1: Use narrow 20 megahertz channels everywhere
Option2: Use wider channels (for example, 80 megahertz) where spectrum is clear and client hardware supports it
Option3: Use only 2.4 GHz channels
Option4: Disable roaming

Q: Which option pairs correctly with its benefit?
Option1: Omnidirectional antenna — long narrow beam for point-to-point
Option2: Directional antenna — focused beam that improves range and signal in the target direction
Option3: Band steering — forces all devices to 2.4 GHz
Option4: Captive portal — provides encryption keys to clients automatically

Q: Which statement about mesh networks and infrastructure networks is accurate?
Option1: Mesh networks require an access point for each client
Option2: Infrastructure networks rely on access points for client access; mesh adds wireless backhaul links between nodes to extend coverage
Option3: Mesh and infrastructure are identical
Option4: Infrastructure networks never use wired connections
